This statement indicates that it is prohibited to take a fast upon oneself. The Gemara answers: This is not difficult. This first ruling, that one who fasts is sacred, is referring to a case where he is able to distress himself without causing bodily harm. column13: And once he reflects upon his failure, repents, and vows to restrain himself, he gains Hashem’s favor, who swears: “Affliction shall not rise up the second time.” For from every suffering endured in this world, an inner vow is etched in the heart never to expand in that specific sin again. In the World to Come, however, the heart of every person will be cleansed, desiring nothing contrary to Hashem, the earth filled with divine knowledge; and this is: “For the mountains shall depart”—meaning the vast occult forces termed sorcery, which in this world appear able to manipulate providence.

column11: At times a person faces a spiritual test of such overwhelming magnitude that it is virtually impossible for him not to sin, in the spirit of the Sages' words (Berakhot 32a): "What can the son do and not sin, etc.?", and in such a state it is legally deemed absolute duress (ones gamur), from which the Merciful One exempts him. And even under the incitement of the evil inclination of such immense ferocity that it cannot be conquered, duress applies and if the Blessed Name turned his heart, then this sin is not a sin at all, but rather the will of the Blessed Name unfolded thus.
column13: Yet just as an established state of prayer is forged from repetitive prayers, so from this permanent state of prayer the faculty of prayer awakens anew toward novel situations. column9: Megillah 16b: ‘The next line of the song inverts the sequence. This is the principle for all songs in the Bible except for this song, referring to the list of Haman’s sons, and the song listing the kings of Canaan who were defeated by Joshua. These two songs are written in the form of a half brick arranged upon a half brick and a whole brick arranged upon a whole brick, i.e., one stitch of text over another, and one blank space over another. What is the reason that these two songs are written in this anomalous fashion? So that they should never rise from their downfall. Just as a wall that is built in this manner will not stand, so too, these individuals should have no resurgence.’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 9 — The Chanukah Celebration and the Meaning of Dedication, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Megillah 16b) to illuminate his statement here (“for there "miracle" denotes the light radiating in the heart through the supernatural miracle wrought by the Blessed Name. – And so it is written: "To the Jews was light", expounded (Megillah 16b): "'Light' — this is...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, divine service, and the rectification of the heart developed in this discourse of Pri Tzaddik.
column11: And nevertheless, they did not take upon themselves a full festival (yom tov) involving complete cessation of labor for the body, because “we are still the servants of Ahasuerus,” and there was not a complete physical redemption from servitude; since in any event, the essential core of the salvation then was that “the Jews had light...” and so forth, which the Sages expounded at the end of the first chapter of Megillah (16b): this refers to Torah, festival, circumcision, and tefillin; see there.
column13: From this awakens in man the yearning for Hashem's light, stirring an intense cry in the human heart: “How and through what can I approach the light of Hashem, for He is awesome!” And this is why he stated that from there the light was created—meaning the sacred awe radiating from the site of the Temple. And according to the opinion that He cloaked Himself in a garment of pure light from which illumination emerged—the inner meaning is: that light reaches man when he roars within his heart: “Is it conceivable that I am severed, heaven forbid, from the Blessed Name who binds and unifies the entire cosmos unto Himself!”

column9: Megillah 16b: ‘§ The Gemara returns to its explanation of the Megilla. The verse states: “The Jews had light and gladness, and joy and honor” (Esther 8:16). Rav Yehuda said: “Light”; this is referring to the Torah that they once again studied. And similarly it says: “For the mitzva is a lamp and the Torah is light” (Proverbs 6:23). “Gladness” [simḥa]; this is referring to the Festivals that they once again observed. And similarly it says: “And you shall be glad [vesamakhta] on your Festival” (Deuteronomy 16:14). “Joy” [sasson]; this is referring to circumcision, as they once again circumcised their sons. And similarly it says: “I rejoice [sas] at Your word” (Psalms 119:162), which the Sages understood…’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 9 — The Chanukah Celebration and the Meaning of Dedication, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Megillah 16b) to illuminate his statement here (“And so it is written: "To the Jews was light", expounded (Megillah 16b): "'Light' — this is Torah", meaning the Oral Torah, for "Torah is light", and orah ending with a heh points to the Oral Torah, Malchut, "The...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, divine service, and the rectification of the heart developed in this discourse of Pri Tzaddik.
column11: And upon its annulment came 'light'—which is Torah (Megillah 16b); and 'to slay (laharog)'—which causes bereavement and mourning, was inverted into 'gladness (simchah)', which is the antithesis of mourning; wherefore our Sages of blessed memory said (ibid.): “this is Yom Tov (the festival)”, which is the opposite of mourning, for mourning does not apply on a festival, as it is written: 'from mourning to a festival' (Esther 9:22).
column13: Wherefore when promised survival for himself and his sons, it did not occur to his mind that there was room to petition for more. column9: Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 670:2: “Taz (Orach Chayim 670:3, citing the Levush) explains why Purim has an obligation of festive meals (mishteh ve-simchah) whereas Chanukah’s primary obligation is Hallel and praise rather than feasting: on Purim Haman decreed to annihilate the physical bodies of Israel, so the salvation is celebrated with bodily feasting; on Chanukah the Greeks sought to uproot the soul and the Torah while leaving the body intact if Israel assimilated, so the salvation is celebrated through spiritual praise and the light of Torah.” Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 9 — The Chanukah Celebration and the Meaning of Dedication, Rav Tzadok cites this commentary and halakhic exposition (Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 670:2) to illuminate his statement here (“And nevertheless it is written in the Shulchan Aruch (Orach Chayim 670:2): that there is somewhat of a mitzvah in augmenting feasts on Chanukah, for during those days occurred the dedication of the Altar, see there....”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, divine service, and the rectification of the heart developed in this discourse of Pri Tzaddik.
column11: And these two sublime faculties are spiritual states operating beyond the physical limbs; unlike mental thought which remains linked to the brain as a physical bodily organ; for these two higher levels transcend the body, termed in the Shulchan Aruch (Orach Chayim 98:1) "the stripping away of corporeality" (hitpashtut hagashmiyut); wherein reaching these rungs one loses all physical awareness of the body, as recorded of Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat (Eruvin 54b) who embodied "be you ravished always with her love" [Proverbs 5:19].
column13: For the supreme revelation of Hashem's greatness in this world is that He cloaked His light in garments of darkness, yet the light breaks through every veil; therefore one who partakes of physical bounty as the nations do, taking without restraint and without a blessing— which alludes to the years of youthful expansiveness in a person before attaining maturity— and afterward the Blessed Name grants him the conscious wisdom to praise Him for it; for upon sight alone one does not recite a blessing over sustenance, but only upon tasting, even though while tasting one is momentarily distracted.

Another matter, “the voice is the voice of Jacob” – Jacob rules only with his voice. “The voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau” – Esau rules only with his hands. Another matter, “the voice is the voice of Jacob” – Rabbi Pinḥas said: The voice of Jacob withdraws into itself. suggests that the fact that the word hakol is without a vav it can be read as if the voice of…’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 9 — The Chanukah Celebration and the Meaning of Dedication, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Bereshit Rabbah 65) to illuminate his statement here (“as written (Bereishit Rabbah 65 and see Menachot 87a), it is possible that there was meat of an olive's volume (kezayit) for every member of the tribe; – and we find regarding the Showbread: "An olive's volume — one...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, divine service, and the rectification of the heart developed in this discourse of Pri Tzaddik.
column11: And the explanation of this is as I wrote elsewhere: that the four zoological categories: domestic animals, beasts, birds, and fish— correspond to Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and David: the wild beast corresponds to Abraham, whose fat (chelev)—meaning the choicest—is kosher to eat; and therefore Abraham did not love Ishmael as intensely as Isaac loved Esau, for under uncompromising justice who can stand, etc., and this is not the place to elaborate.
column13: As elucidated in Mei HaShiloach (Vol. 1, Noach, s.v. Vayihyu Yemei Terach) on Bereishit Rabbah 39:7: “The Holy One said to Abraham: You I exempt from honoring father and mother, but I do not exempt another from honoring father and mother” (examine there).

column9: Menachot 87a: ‘GEMARA: The Gemara cites a baraita that clarifies Rabbi Meir’s opinion. column11: And Purim clarifies the indestructible root of Israel: that even while they appear trapped in evil—it is not their ultimate Truth; this revelation shall never be annulled, for this is a unique category holding no parallel with other festivals nor with all future redemptions. For every other redemption is an exodus from evil into good; whereas Purim is not merely an exodus into good, but the revelation that even while appearing evil—the Jew is not evil at all.
column13: And this is what Midrash Rabbah teaches: Had it said “God created heaven and earth,” I would have thought heaven and earth are deities; therefore it states “et.” The explanation of this is: the word “et” denotes a slight interval separating the primordial Will from the manifest revelation of creation; and heaven is merely a garment for His simple, absolute Will; for the word “et” is enfolded within “Zot” (This)—the mystery of midnight, whence all spiritual bounties issue—and “et” cleaves directly to the Emanator.

column9: Zohar, Terumah 2:12-4:23: “In the Zohar (Terumah II 127a, 180a), the four directions of the world and the vessels of the Tabernacle are aligned with the four camps of the Shekhinah and the Primordial Light that shines from East, South, North, and West.” Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 9 — The Chanukah Celebration and the Meaning of Dedication, Rav Tzadok cites this kabbalistic teaching (Zohar, Terumah 2:12-4:23) to illuminate his statement here (“and it states in the Holy Zohar (Part II, 127a bottom): "When it is concealed and hidden within, inside the Supernal Light above, then it stands in the form of the letter Samech, etc.", – – meaning that the...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, divine service, and the rectification of the heart developed in this discourse of Pri Tzaddik.
column11: Next, the western direction (Ma'arav) corresponds to the Heart: as taught in the Mishnah in Berakhot (28b): "one should direct his heart toward the Holy of Holies"; as expounded in the Zohar, that the human heart aligns directly opposite the Holy of Holies where the Shechinah rests in the west; because authentic awe is awakened through the inner realization of "I set Hashem before me always," as codified in the Rema's gloss at the opening of Orach Chaim.
column13: For in truth the primordial light was concealed by the Blessed Name, as the Zohar states (Bereishit 47a): “And through what does man merit that light? Through the Torah”; as taught in the Zohar (Shemot 15b) that Hashem embedded the light within Torah, such that whenever Israel toils in Torah, a measure of that primordial light is unveiled.

column9: Chagigah 12a: ‘The Gemara answers: This should be understood in accordance with Rabbi Elazar, as Rabbi Elazar said: The light that the Holy One, Blessed be He, created on the first day was not that of the sun but a different kind of light, through which man could observe from one end of the world to the other. But when the Holy One, Blessed be He, looked upon the generation of the Flood and the generation of the Dispersion and saw that their ways were corrupt and that they might misuse this light for evil, He arose and concealed it from them, as it is stated: “And from the wicked their light is withheld” (Job 38:15).’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 9 — The Chanukah Celebration and the Meaning of Dedication, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Chagigah 12a) to illuminate his statement here (“which is the light that is "good" (and this was explained on Rosh Chodesh Kislev); and this is the unique sanctity of this month, and at its end we merit the light that is "good", the light of the First Day hidden...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, divine service, and the rectification of the heart developed in this discourse of Pri Tzaddik.
column11: For in truth they perceived that Havayah is Elohim, the God of Israel, and that all modes of awe among the Children of Israel derive from Hashem, Blessed be He, it having been His divine Will that one should at times be deliberate and fearful; and this served as the rectification for Phinehas in his misplaced deliberation.
column12: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 3:8 (§2)
column13: For what the Generation of the Flood and Dispersion desired in reckless expansion, that reflected reality before the world was created, when existence was concealed within His essence without any creative renewal; yet from the moment Hashem brought the world from potential to actuality and from concealment to revelation, it was so that Creation from its own side innovate renewal upon the earth, and actively know that Hashem sanctifies them.

And regarding this we plead "Merciful One, etc.," in the spirit of Section 212 regarding Elisha casting the wood: seeing that You answered that person in this matter, save us too even though we are not like him, for what difference does it make to You?
column13: So it is with the Supernal Light: gazing with disciplined stages preserves the cosmic order, whereas gazing recklessly disrupts it, as written of the Seraphim (Isaiah 6:2): “With two he covered his face,” explained in Midrash Tanchuma (Tzav 13): so that he should not gaze directly toward the Shechinah; and though their entire vitality derives from gazing upon the Shechinah, they veil their faces to avoid gazing excessively beyond their spiritual measure.

column11: Now, from the perspective of ultimate Unity there is no room for merit or guilt at all: since one perceives that there is literally nothing besides Him, all human actions are also the actions of the Blessed Name; and concerning this Scripture states: "If you are righteous, what do you give Him, or what does He receive from your hand?", meaning that all is His and His doing, which is true from the vantage of absolute Unity; and as stated in Berakhot [32a]: "Were it not for three verses... 'and whom I have dealt ill with'", etc..
column13: “Of every tree of the garden you may freely eat; but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, you shall not eat of it.” My revered father, the holy Gaon, of blessed memory (Mei HaShiloach, Vol. 1, Bereishit, s.v. Vayetzav), explained: that in the future when the sin of Adam HaRishon is rectified, the syntax of the verses will be joined thus: “Of every tree of the garden you may freely eat, and of the tree of knowledge—the good”; followed by: “and the evil you shall not eat”.

column9: Shabbat 22a: ‘A Hanukkah lamp that one placed above twenty cubits is invalid, just as a sukka whose roofing is more than twenty cubits high, and just as an alleyway whose beam, its symbolic fourth partition in order to place an eiruv, is more than twenty cubits high, are invalid. The reason is the same in all three cases: People do not usually raise their heads and see objects at a height above twenty cubits. As there is a requirement to see all of these, they are deemed invalid when placed above that height. And the Gemara cites another statement that Rav Kahana said that Rav Natan bar Manyumi taught in the name of Rav Tanḥum: What is the meaning of the verse that is written with regard to Joseph:…’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 10 — The Chanukah Lamp, the Mezuzah, and the Light of Torah, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Shabbat 22a) to illuminate his statement here (“In the Gemara (Shabbat 22a): "The Chanukah candle is on the left, the mezuzah on the right." The matter is according to what we explained in the name of the Ramban (beginning of Parashat Beha'alotecha) who explained...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, divine service, and the rectification of the heart developed in this discourse of Pri Tzaddik.

column13: Which is more grave? One who says to the king: “Either I or you in the palace,” or one who says: “I in the palace and not you!” Yet the Flood generation, being immersed in robbery, left no remnant; while the Dispersion, loving one another, left an enduring remnant. Meaning, in its theological depth the failure of the Dispersion was far graver than that of the Flood: for the Dispersion acted with calculated obstinacy to force Hashem's presence to dwell among their impurities, as though waging war and conquering Him (like sorcery that diminishes the heavenly entourage, Chullin 7b)—which is saying to the King: “I and not you.”

column9: Ramban on Numbers 8:2: “‘Speak unto Aaron, and say unto him: When you light the lamps, the seven lamps shall give light in front of the candlestick’ (Numbers 8:2): Ramban quotes the Midrash Rabbah that Hashem comforted Aaron when he saw the dedication offerings of the twelve tribal Princes, promising him: ‘By your life, yours is greater than theirs—for the sacrifices operate only while the Temple stands, whereas your lamps (referring to the Hasmonean dedication of the Chanukah lights) will shine forever.’” Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 10 — The Chanukah Lamp, the Mezuzah, and the Light of Torah, Rav Tzadok cites this commentary and halakhic exposition (Ramban on Numbers 8:2) to illuminate his statement here (“The matter is according to what we explained in the name of the Ramban (beginning of Parashat Beha'alotecha) who explained what is written in the Midrash Rabbah there: that He said to Aaron: "For greater than this...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, divine service, and the rectification of the heart developed in this discourse of Pri Tzaddik.
column11: But there it does not deal with protection from physical retribution (haganah mi-pur'anus), but rather with rescue from sin and the yetzer hara; as explained in the passage there, that both according to Rav Yosef and according to Rava it is regarding this that they distinguish between Torah and mitzvah (whether while actively engaged or when not actively engaged); and on this they stated the rationale that "sin extinguishes": for protection occurs because a mitzvah draws another mitzvah, whereas a sin draws another sin, extinguishing the spiritual momentum of the corresponding mitzvah so that he remains balanced in his free choice.
column13: “And God said, Let there be light.” To understand: why was it written “and there was light”? For when the Blessed Name commanded, surely it was done! Rather, it is as stated in the Holy Zohar (Balak 192b): The Holy One, blessed be He, leaped to the place that was needed, and the matter was explained (in Parashat Vezot Haberakhah) that the Blessed Name looked ahead to see what would endure after He withdrew from this garment.

column9: Bava Metzia 59b: ‘Rabbi Yehoshua stood on his feet and said: It is written: “It is not in heaven” (Deuteronomy 30:12). Since the majority of Rabbis disagreed with Rabbi Eliezer’s opinion, the halakha is not ruled in accordance with his opinion. The Gemara relates: Years after, Rabbi Natan encountered Elijah the prophet and said to him: What did the Holy One, Blessed be He, do at that time, when Rabbi Yehoshua issued his…’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 10 — The Chanukah Lamp, the Mezuzah, and the Light of Torah, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Bava Metzia 59b) to illuminate his statement here (“and as written (Bava Metzia 59b) that the Holy One said: "My children have triumphed over Me", and it states (Chagigah 15b): "That He states teachings from the mouth of all the Rabbis, but from the mouth of Rabbi...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, divine service, and the rectification of the heart developed in this discourse of Pri Tzaddik.
column11: Whereas had Ahab's men discovered him, they would have forced him to revoke the decree, as happened later and as Jehoram did to Elisha. And concerning this it is stated: "It is not in heaven" (Deuteronomy 30:12); and even though they assisted Rabbi Eliezer through supernatural miracles to show the law was according to him, the Sages did not rely upon it (Bava Metzia 59b), for they reasoned that the miracle occurred merely because he desired to walk in that path.
column13: Having grasped the root failure of the first generation and endured the suffering of the Flood. And this is the basis of the law linking the curse of one who retracts his word to the Generation of the Flood, as in Bava Metzia (44a): If one gave money but did not yet draw the produce, he may legally retract; yet the Sages declared: “He who took retribution from the Generation of the Flood and the Generation of the Dispersion will take retribution from him who does not stand by his word.”

column9: Chagigah 15b: ‘The Gemara relates: Rabba bar Sheila found Elijah the prophet, who had appeared to him. He said to Elijah: What is the Holy One, Blessed be He, doing? Elijah said to him: He is stating halakhot transmitted by all of the Sages, but in the name of Rabbi Meir He will not speak. He said to him: Why? He replied: Because he learned halakhot from the mouth of Aḥer. He said to him: Why should he be judged unfavorably for that? Rabbi Meir found a pomegranate and ate its contents while throwing away its peel. He said to him: Indeed, your defense has been heard above. Now God is saying: My son, Meir, says: When a person suffers, e.g., by receiving lashes or the death penalty at the hands of the…’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 10 — The Chanukah Lamp, the Mezuzah, and the Light of Torah, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Chagigah 15b) to illuminate his statement here (“and it states (Chagigah 15b): "That He states teachings from the mouth of all the Rabbis, but from the mouth of Rabbi Meir He does not, etc.; now He says: Meir My son says, etc." And this began from the Men of the...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, divine service, and the rectification of the heart developed in this discourse of Pri Tzaddik.
column11: And was not Acher likewise filled with Torah, seeing that Rabbi Meir learned from his mouth and ate his inner fruit (Chagigah 15b)? And in the Gemara [ibid. 15a] it is explicitly stated that solely because of the proclamation "except for Acher" did he say: "Let me at least enjoy this world"; therefore what they said—that he intended to rebel, meaning to spite Heaven, which falls under the category of heretics (Rosh Hashanah 17a) where Gehinnom is consumed—that was only at the beginning when he uttered the heresy of "two independent powers".
column13: The first Decalogue, however, was spoken prior to the sin directly from the mouth of the Blessed Name in immense illumination, as the commandments exist at their root in lucid clarity; and from Hashem's perspective all opposites are inherently united, wherefore they appear without a Vav, as in the Zohar (Emor 93b): “A Vav is not found Above.”

column9: Bereshit Rabbah 2: ‘Rabbi Yehuda bar Simon interpreted the verses regarding the generations. “The earth was emptiness and disorder” – this is Adam the first man, who became oblivion and nothingness. “And disorder” – this is Cain, who sought to restore the world to emptiness and disorder. “And darkness” – this is the generation of Enosh, 23:7). based on the verse: “Their actions are in the dark and they say: Who sees us and who knows of us?” (Isaiah 29:15). “Upon the face of the depths” – this is the generation of the Flood, as it is stated: “On that day all the wellsprings of the great depths were breached” (Genesis 7:11). “And the spirit [ruaḥ] of God was hovering over the surface of the water” – based on…’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 10 — The Chanukah Lamp, the Mezuzah, and the Light of Torah, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Bereshit Rabbah 2) to illuminate his statement here (“for their intellectual wisdom is called "darkness" and not light, – and as our Sages of blessed memory said (Bereishit Rabbah, Parashah 2): "'And darkness' — this is the kingdom of Greece, etc."”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, divine service, and the rectification of the heart developed in this discourse of Pri Tzaddik.
column11: When a person walks from bright light into slight darkness, he cannot see initially; but if he remains there for some time, he begins to see. Therefore, when a person is born he lacks mature discernment until he grows up. And one who abides continuously in slight darkness acclimates and sees well therein; and this explains why one who studied and then abandoned the path is harsher than an ordinary ignorant person Pesachim 49b, for "a mitzvah is a candle, and the Torah is light" Proverbs 6:23, and our Sages stated Sotah 21a that the Torah is likened to a great blazing torch.
column12: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 2:1
column13: "And Hashem said to Avram: Go for yourself, etc., to the land that I will show you," (Genesis 12:1), "For I will pour water upon the thirsty, and streams upon the dry land; I will pour My spirit upon your seed, and My blessing upon your offspring" (Isaiah 44:3). column9: Berakhot 54a: ‘The mishna articulates a general principle: One is obligated to recite a blessing for the bad that befalls him just as he recites a blessing for the good that befalls him, as it is stated: “And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might” (Deuteronomy 6:5). column9: Shabbat 89b: ‘We learned in the mishna: From where is it derived that one ties a scarlet strip of wool to the scapegoat?
